system:
You are an art-world editor compiling a gallery guide for New York, United States. Answer with the
JSON object the schema describes and nothing else. Rank by significance and influence in the
contemporary art world: programme quality, the artists represented, art-fair presence, critical and
institutional attention, and longevity. Include commercial galleries and the nonprofit, artist-run and
project spaces that show contemporary art to the public in New York itself (galleries whose home is
elsewhere count only through a permanent New York space). Exclude museums, art fairs, auction houses,
framers, art schools, decor shops, online-only dealers and advisories. For every gallery give its usual
name; its official website when you are confident of it, else null; the district it is in, using one of
these labels when it fits (Chelsea, Downtown, Uptown, Brooklyn/Queens, Hamptons) else the district name you know; a street address hint when you
know it (street and number are enough), else null; its kind (gallery, museum, nonprofit, project_space, university, other); and a short note on why it
matters. Every entry must be a distinct venue — list a gallery with several New York spaces once.
user: What are the 100 most significant and influential galleries in New York, ranked in order? If less than 100 significant galleries exist, provide the complete list of significant galleries.

galleries.name: Gagosian
galleries.note: The world's largest gallery network, with multiple New York spaces; blue-chip estates, market-defining exhibitions and museum-scale shows.

galleries.name: David Zwirner
galleries.note: Global mega-gallery with scholarly catalogues, major estates (Ruscha, Yayoi Kusama, Bourgeois) and a Chelsea campus plus uptown and Tribeca spaces.

galleries.name: Pace
galleries.note: Founded 1960; eight-storey flagship, deep postwar holdings and a strong technology/immersive art programme.

galleries.name: Hauser & Wirth
galleries.note: Museum-quality historical surveys and estates (Guston, Nevelson, Bourgeois) alongside leading living artists.

galleries.name: Marian Goodman Gallery
galleries.note: Brought European conceptualism to New York since 1977; Gerhard Richter, Steve McQueen, William Kentridge, Tacita Dean.

galleries.name: Matthew Marks Gallery
galleries.note: A pillar of Chelsea since the early 1990s; Nan Goldin, Robert Gober, Ellsworth Kelly estate.

galleries.name: Paula Cooper Gallery
galleries.note: SoHo's first gallery (1968) and a minimalism/conceptualism standard-bearer: Sol LeWitt, Carl Andre, Sherrie Levine.

galleries.name: Gladstone Gallery
galleries.note: Rigorous conceptual and installation-based programme: Matthew Barney, Anicka Yi, Carrie Mae Weems; absorbed Gavin Brown's roster.

galleries.name: Luhring Augustine
galleries.note: Since 1985; Rachel Whiteread, Christopher Wool, Ragnar Kjartansson, with Bushwick and Tribeca outposts.

galleries.name: Lisson Gallery
galleries.note: London institution's New York flagship; conceptual and land-art legacies plus Ai Weiwei, Carmen Herrera estate.

galleries.name: Petzel Gallery
galleries.note: Critically driven programme rooted in the Pictures generation and German conceptualism; Wade Guyton, Charline von Heyl.

galleries.name: Greene Naftali
galleries.note: One of Chelsea's most consistently experimental programmes; Jacqueline Humphries, Paul Chan, Rachel Harrison.

galleries.name: 303 Gallery
galleries.note: Lisa Spellman's gallery since 1984; Doug Aitken, Karen Kilimnik, Alicja Kwade, Stephen Shore.

galleries.name: Sean Kelly
galleries.note: Marina Abramović, Kehinde Wiley and Antony Gormley; strong institutional placement and performance history.

galleries.name: Casey Kaplan
galleries.note: Sharp mid-career programme: Jordan Casteel, Kevin Beasley, Sarah Crowner, Giorgio Griffa.

galleries.name: Andrew Kreps Gallery
galleries.note: Influential Tribeca dealer with a research-driven roster and rediscoveries; Roe Ethridge, Camille Henrot, Corita Kent estate.

galleries.name: Anton Kern Gallery
galleries.note: Townhouse gallery with a wry, painting-strong roster: Nicole Eisenman, Chris Martin, Wilhelm Sasnal.

galleries.name: Jack Shainman Gallery
galleries.address_hint: 513 West 20th Street; The Clocktower, 46 Lafayette Street
galleries.note: Decades of championing Black and diasporic artists: Kerry James Marshall, El Anatsui, Nick Cave, Carrie Mae Weems.

galleries.name: Perrotin
galleries.note: French global gallery's New York outposts; Takashi Murakami, JR, Daniel Arsham and a heavy fair presence.

galleries.name: Lehmann Maupin
galleries.note: Internationally minded roster: Do Ho Suh, Teresita Fernández, Nari Ward, Cecilia Vicuña.

galleries.name: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery
galleries.note: Olafur Eliasson, Mark Dion, Analia Saban; a bellwether for installation and ecological practice since 1994.

galleries.name: James Cohan
galleries.address_hint: 48 Walker Street / 52 Walker Street area, Tribeca
galleries.note: Global roster with strong Asian and diasporic representation; Firelei Báez, Trenton Doyle Hancock, Bill Viola estate.

galleries.name: Marianne Boesky Gallery
galleries.note: Since 1996; Frank Stella, Donald Moffett, Sanford Biggers and the Ghada Amer market.

galleries.name: Sperone Westwater
galleries.note: Founded 1975 to bring Arte Povera and European postwar art to New York; Foster + Partners building on the Bowery.

galleries.name: Karma
galleries.note: Fast-rising East Village gallery and publisher; Reggie Burrows Hodges, Maja Ruznic, Gertrude Abercrombie estate.

galleries.name: Salon 94
galleries.note: Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn's genre-crossing programme of design, ceramics and contemporary art in a landmark mansion.

galleries.name: Bortolami
galleries.note: Tribeca anchor with the innovative Artist/City project; Daniel Buren, Barbara Kasten, Eric Wesley.

galleries.name: White Cube
galleries.note: The influential London gallery's 2023 New York flagship, bringing Tracey Emin, Julie Mehretu and Theaster Gates uptown.

galleries.name: Galerie Buchholz
galleries.note: Cologne/Berlin gallery's cerebral uptown space; Wolfgang Tillmans, Isa Genzken, Danh Vo.

galleries.name: kurimanzutto
galleries.note: Mexico City's leading gallery in New York; Gabriel Orozco, Minerva Cuevas, Haegue Yang.

galleries.name: Skarstedt
galleries.note: Secondary-market powerhouse for 1980s-90s American and European art; Condo, Prince, Sherman, Kippenberger.

galleries.name: Kasmin
galleries.note: Multiple Chelsea spaces plus a rooftop sculpture garden on the High Line; Lee Krasner and Robert Indiana estates.

galleries.name: Lévy Gorvy Dayan
galleries.note: Scholarly secondary-market exhibitions in a Beaux-Arts townhouse; Bourgeois, Zao Wou-Ki, Günther Uecker.

galleries.name: Mnuchin Gallery
galleries.note: Museum-grade postwar surveys (David Hammons, Agnes Martin) and a major secondary-market presence.

galleries.name: Acquavella Galleries
galleries.note: Three generations of dealing modern masters, now with contemporary shows by Damian Loeb, Wayne Thiebaud estate.

galleries.name: P·P·O·W
galleries.note: Since 1983 a home for politically engaged and queer art: David Wojnarowicz estate, Martin Wong, Carolee Schneemann.

galleries.name: Sikkema Malloy Jenkins
galleries.note: Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Amy Sillman; consistently museum-facing programme over three decades.

galleries.name: Galerie Lelong & Co.
galleries.note: International roster with strong Latin American and feminist holdings: Ana Mendieta estate, Zarina, Alfredo Jaar.

galleries.name: Alexander Gray Associates
galleries.note: Rigorous focus on conceptual, feminist and social-practice legacies: Melvin Edwards, Lorraine O'Grady, Joan Semmel.

galleries.name: Miguel Abreu Gallery
galleries.note: Theory-driven Lower East Side programme with publishing arm Sequence Press; R. H. Quaytman, Sam Lewitt.

galleries.name: Bridget Donahue
galleries.note: Small space with outsized critical clout; Martine Syms, Susan Cianciolo, Lorraine O'Grady collaborations.

galleries.name: 47 Canal
galleries.note: Defined a generation of post-internet and diasporic practice; Anicka Yi, Josh Kline, Michele Abeles.

galleries.name: Bureau
galleries.note: Lower East Side gallery with a quietly influential roster and steady museum placements.

galleries.name: Company Gallery
galleries.note: Vital platform for queer and trans artists; Jesse Darling, Elle Pérez, Marilyn Minter collaborations.

galleries.name: Reena Spaulings Fine Art
galleries.note: Artist-run gallery-as-artwork since 2004; a conceptual node for the downtown scene and Bernadette Corporation circle.

galleries.name: CANADA
galleries.note: Artist-founded, painting-forward and scene-defining since 1999; Katherine Bernhardt, Joe Bradley alumni.

galleries.name: Chapter NY
galleries.note: Sharp emerging programme that has launched several now-major painters into institutional shows.

galleries.name: Gordon Robichaux
galleries.note: Curatorially adventurous gallery mixing intergenerational, queer and outsider practices; frequent biennial picks.

galleries.name: CLEARING
galleries.note: Brooklyn-born, now Bowery-based; incubator for Harold Ancart, Loie Hollowell, Calvin Marcus.

galleries.name: Maxwell Graham (Essex Street)
galleries.note: Fiercely conceptual programme and archival rediscoveries; a critics' favourite with strong museum traction.

galleries.name: Nicelle Beauchene Gallery
galleries.note: Consistent championing of women artists and craft-inflected practice since 2009.

galleries.name: Derek Eller Gallery
galleries.note: Long-running downtown dealer known for idiosyncratic painting and self-taught rediscoveries.

galleries.name: kaufmann repetto
galleries.note: Milan gallery's New York space; Latifa Echakhch, Andrea Bowers, Judith Hopf.

galleries.name: Almine Rech
galleries.note: International gallery with a Picasso-linked history and a broad contemporary painting roster.

galleries.name: Massimo De Carlo
galleries.note: Major Italian gallery's New York outpost; Rudolf Stingel, Carsten Höller, Sanya Kantarovsky.

galleries.name: Mendes Wood DM
galleries.note: São Paulo gallery's townhouse space bringing Brazilian and global-south artists to New York.

galleries.name: 52 Walker
galleries.note: Ebony L. Haynes's independently curated Tribeca space, among the most critically watched programmes in the city.

galleries.name: Jeffrey Deitch
galleries.note: Spectacle-driven SoHo shows and street-art crossovers from a dealer who shaped the 1990s and 2000s.

galleries.name: Venus Over Manhattan
galleries.note: Adam Lindemann's gallery for eccentric historical rediscoveries and buzzy contemporary pairings.

galleries.name: Nicola Vassell Gallery
galleries.note: Opened 2021 with an ambitious programme foregrounding Black artists and photography; rapid institutional uptake.

galleries.name: Tina Kim Gallery
galleries.note: Key conduit for Korean art in New York, including Dansaekhwa figures and Ghada Amer.

galleries.name: Michael Werner Gallery
galleries.note: Historic advocate of German postwar painting — Baselitz, Polke, Kirkeby — in an Upper East Side townhouse.

galleries.name: Yancey Richardson Gallery
galleries.note: Leading contemporary photography dealer; Mickalene Thomas, Zanele Muholi, Andrew Moore.

galleries.name: Howard Greenberg Gallery
galleries.note: The definitive New York address for classic and documentary photography, with strong museum ties.

galleries.name: Bruce Silverstein Gallery
galleries.note: Photography-centred programme bridging modernist estates and contemporary lens-based practice.

galleries.name: Andrew Edlin Gallery
galleries.note: Foremost dealer of self-taught and outsider art; founder of the Outsider Art Fair, with Henry Darger estate.

galleries.name: Ortuzar
galleries.note: Historically minded Tribeca gallery reviving overlooked conceptual figures alongside contemporary artists.

galleries.name: Peter Freeman, Inc.
galleries.note: Quietly authoritative programme spanning Mel Bochner, Thomas Schütte and drawing-focused historical shows.

galleries.name: David Nolan Gallery
galleries.note: Drawing-centred connoisseurship; Barry Le Va, Jorinde Voigt, German postwar works on paper.

galleries.name: Craig F. Starr Gallery
galleries.note: Small, scholarly exhibitions of postwar American art that routinely earn outsized critical notice.

galleries.name: Susan Inglett Gallery
galleries.note: Politically committed programme and editions expertise; Beverly Semmes, Guerrilla Girls projects.

galleries.name: Garth Greenan Gallery
galleries.note: Reappraisals of postwar American artists, notably Native American and women artists such as Jaune Quick-to-See Smith.

galleries.name: Magenta Plains
galleries.note: Intergenerational Lower East Side programme linking downtown veterans with younger conceptualists.

galleries.name: Rachel Uffner Gallery
galleries.note: Lower East Side mainstay since 2008 with a strong record of launching women painters and ceramicists.

galleries.name: Jack Hanley Gallery
galleries.note: Bay Area transplant with a long history of spotting emerging talent early.

galleries.name: Klaus von Nichtssagend Gallery
galleries.note: Brooklyn-founded, artist-friendly gallery with a durable experimental programme.

galleries.name: Simone Subal Gallery
galleries.note: European-inflected conceptual programme and rediscoveries of Austrian and feminist avant-gardes.

galleries.name: Broadway
galleries.note: Tribeca gallery that has quickly become a fixture of the emerging-scene circuit and fair rosters.

galleries.name: Ramiken
galleries.note: Nomadic, risk-taking gallery known for raw installations and cult artists such as Andra Ursuta alumni projects.

galleries.name: Downs & Ross
galleries.note: Lower East Side gallery with an international, research-based emerging programme.

galleries.name: Lomex
galleries.note: Subcultural, art-historically curious programme influential among younger critics and curators.

galleries.name: Nathalie Karg Gallery
galleries.note: Sculpture-strong downtown gallery run by a veteran dealer, with steady fair presence.

galleries.name: Timothy Taylor
galleries.note: London gallery's Tribeca space; transatlantic painting programme and estate representation.

galleries.name: Half Gallery
galleries.note: Bill Powers's nimble gallery, an early stop for many now-prominent figurative painters.

galleries.name: Harper's
galleries.note: Fast-growing gallery with New York and Hamptons spaces and a widely watched emerging-painting programme.

galleries.name: Nahmad Contemporary
galleries.note: Ambitious curated historical exhibitions backed by one of the market's great modern collections.

galleries.name: Michael Rosenfeld Gallery
galleries.note: Central to the reappraisal of twentieth-century African American artists; Norman Lewis and Beauford Delaney estates.

galleries.name: Fierman
galleries.note: Small Lower East Side space with a queer, subversive programme and loyal critical following.

galleries.name: Theta
galleries.note: Young Tribeca gallery praised for tightly conceived shows by emerging conceptual artists.

galleries.name: The Journal Gallery
galleries.note: Grew out of the artist-run magazine; Tribeca space with an influential, design-savvy programme.

galleries.name: Swiss Institute
galleries.note: Free-admission kunsthalle whose exhibitions and architecture commissions shape the downtown discourse.

galleries.name: Artists Space
galleries.note: Founded 1972; the alternative space that launched the Pictures generation and still sets the critical agenda.

galleries.name: White Columns
galleries.note: New York's oldest alternative space, with a curated artist registry that feeds the entire gallery ecosystem.

galleries.name: The Kitchen
galleries.note: Historic incubator for video, performance and experimental music since 1971.

galleries.name: SculptureCenter
galleries.note: Maillart-converted trolley repair shop presenting career-making commissions by emerging sculptors.

galleries.name: The Drawing Center
galleries.note: The only US institution devoted to drawing; influential historical and contemporary exhibitions since 1977.

galleries.name: Pioneer Works
galleries.note: Large-scale Brooklyn cultural centre combining exhibitions, residencies, science and music programming.

galleries.name: Participant Inc
galleries.note: Lower East Side alternative space with a defining record in queer, performance and AIDS-era art histories.

galleries.name: Printed Matter
galleries.note: The world's leading nonprofit for artists' books, with exhibitions and the NY Art Book Fair.

galleries.name: Amant
galleries.note: Ambitious, well-resourced Brooklyn art centre with residencies and internationally curated exhibitions.
